A.explanation: Too small by a factor of 1000, from confusing $\text{ms}$ with $\mu\text{s}$ when converting the time-base to seconds.

B.explanation: Too small by a factor of 1000, from using milliseconds as microseconds so $50\text{ ms}$ is treated as $50 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$.

C.explanation: Half the correct period, from counting about 7 oscillations instead of 3.5 complete cycles in the $10.0\text{ cm}$ trace.

D.explanation: Total time $50\text{ ms}$ divided by $3.5$ complete cycles gives about $14\times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 1.4\times 10^{-2}\text{ s}$.

hints: Notice the horizontal axis is time: $5\text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ means every $1\text{ cm}$ of the $10.0\text{ cm}$ trace represents $5\text{ ms}$.
Count how many complete sine-wave cycles fit in the $10.0\text{ cm}$ length, remembering the trace starts part-way up and ends part-way down so it is $3.5$ periods, not $3$ or $4$.
Divide the total time for the whole $10.0\text{ cm}$ screen by the number of cycles, then convert $\text{ms}$ to $\text{s}$ with $1\text{ ms}=10^{-3}\text{ s}$.
walkthrough: Find the total time represented by the whole trace. Time-base $= 5\text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ and length $= 10.0\text{ cm}$, so total time $= 10.0 \times 5 = 50\text{ ms}$.
Count the number of complete periods shown. The trace contains 3 full sine waves plus one extra half-wave, giving $N = 3.5$ cycles.
Use period $T = \frac{\text{total time}}{N}$. So $T = \frac{50\text{ ms}}{3.5} \approx 14.3\text{ ms}$.
Convert to seconds: $14.3\text{ ms} = 14.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}$.
